subject: radiology
title: Computed Tomography Principles: Hounsfield Units, Generations, and Helical CT

steps.title: The Hounsfield Unit Scale
steps.tx: **Hounsfield unit scale** quantifies tissue radiodensity relative to distilled water. Formulated by Sir Godfrey Hounsfield, the CT number is calculated as 1000 multiplied by the linear attenuation coefficient of tissue minus that of water, divided by that of water. Distilled water serves as the central anchor at 0 HU, air measures minus 1000 HU, and dense cortical bone reaches plus 1000 HU.

nodes.label: Divide by water coefficient and multiply by 1000

steps.tx: Every CT number is a comparison with water wearing a numerical scale. The **Hounsfield scale** sets water at zero, air near minus one thousand, fat below zero, soft tissue modestly positive and cortical bone in the high hundreds and beyond. Reading a scan begins by placing each grey structure on that line. A region of interest measurement ends arguments about whether a lesion is fat, fluid or soft tissue in seconds.
steps.say: Hounsfield units run from air at minus one thousand through water at zero to dense bone. Measuring a region settles tissue arguments quickly.

steps.title: Biological Tissue CT Numbers
steps.tx: **Tissue CT attenuation values** characterize human pathology through numerical ranges. Acute clotted hematoma measures 50 to 80 HU due to concentrated globin proteins, distinguishing it from circulating unclotted blood at 30 to 45 HU. Simple serous fluid measures 0 to 15 HU, subcutaneous and retroperitoneal adipose tissue measures minus 50 to minus 100 HU, and normal aerated lung parenchyma measures minus 700 to minus 900 HU.

steps.title: First and Second Generation CT
steps.tx: **Translate-rotate CT geometry** defined the earliest scanners developed in the 1970s. First-generation units used a single pencil beam coupled to one or two sodium iodide detectors, translating across the patient before indexing by one degree, requiring 4.5 to 5 minutes per slice. Second-generation scanners introduced a narrow 10-degree fan beam with a linear detector array of up to 30 detectors, reducing scan time to 18 seconds.

left.title: First-Generation Scanners (1972)
points: Single pencil beam with 1 or 2 detectors
Scan time of 4.5 to 5 minutes per single slice

right.title: Second-Generation Scanners (1975)
points: Narrow 10-degree fan beam with up to 30 detectors
Translate-rotate motion with larger angular steps
Scan time reduced to approximately 18 seconds per slice

steps.title: Third and Fourth Generation Architecture
steps.tx: **Rotate-rotate CT design** characterizes third-generation systems, where a wide 40 to 50-degree fan beam and curved detector array rotate synchronously around the patient in under one second. A malfunctioning detector creates circular ring artefacts. Fourth-generation scanners overcame ring artefacts by placing the X-ray tube rotating inside a continuous stationary 360-degree ring of thousands of fixed detectors, though at higher mechanical cost.

left.title: Third Generation (Rotate-Rotate)
points: Tube and curved detector rotate synchronously
Scan time under 0.3 seconds; dominant modern architecture
Susceptible to ring artefacts if single detector drifts

right.title: Fourth Generation (Rotate-Stationary)
points: Rotating tube inside fixed 360-degree detector ring
Completely immune to detector ring artefacts
High cost and complex geometry limited adoption

steps.title: Helical Volumetric Acquisition
steps.tx: **Helical spiral CT acquisition** was made possible by electromechanical slip-ring technology, which eliminated winding high-tension cables and enabled continuous gantry rotation. As the X-ray tube spins continuously, the patient couch feeds smoothly through the gantry bore at constant velocity. This traces an uninterrupted helical path through the patient, creating a seamless volumetric data set that prevents respiratory misregistration between adjacent slices.

steps.title: Helical Pitch Dynamics
steps.tx: **Helical scan pitch** defines the relationship between patient table movement and X-ray beam collimation, calculated as table advancement per 360-degree rotation divided by total beam collimation width. A pitch of 1.0 represents contiguous scanning. A pitch below 1.0 overlaps adjacent data loops, improving longitudinal z-axis resolution at the cost of higher patient dose, whereas a pitch above 1.0 accelerates coverage.

steps.title: Window Width Contrast Modulation
steps.tx: **Window width contrast control** manages the displayed greyscale contrast on diagnostic monitors. While CT detectors capture thousands of discrete attenuation levels, human vision discerns only 16 to 32 shades of grey. Window width sets the total span of Hounsfield units mapped across display greyscale from black to white. Narrow window widths dramatically enhance contrast between tissues possessing nearly identical densities.

left.title: Narrow Window Width (WW 80)
points: Spans small range of Hounsfield units
Steep greyscale slope accentuates subtle density differences
Standard brain window distinguishes grey and white matter

right.title: Wide Window Width (WW 1500)
points: Spans wide range of Hounsfield units
Gentle slope accommodates extreme tissue disparities
Standard bone and lung windows visualize trabeculae and vessels

steps.tx: The same scan data can be repainted for brain, lung or bone by moving two controls. **Window width and level** choose which slice of Hounsfield values stretches across the visible greys: narrow windows at low levels for brain detail, wide high windows for lung and bone. Everything outside the chosen range clips to black or white and vanishes. A lesion missed on one window may be obvious on another, so window discipline is diagnostic skill.
steps.say: Window width and level select which Hounsfield range fills the grey scale for brain, lung or bone. Checking several windows is diagnostic skill.

vis.alt: Schematic of CT window width and level mapping greyscale for brain, lung and bone windows.
vis.caption: Three greyscale mappings show the same data windowed for brain, lung and bone. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: Window Level Midpoint Selection
steps.tx: **Window level center** positions the central midpoint of the displayed greyscale range at the exact attenuation value of the tissue under clinical examination. Attenuation values falling below the window floor display as pure black, while those above the ceiling display as pure white. Radiologists select window level plus 35 HU for brain parenchyma, minus 600 HU for aerated lung, and plus 400 HU for bone.
